title: Skill2Query: Exploiting Skill Structure to Generate Pseudo-Queries for Agent Skill Retrieval

analysis.tldr: Skill2Query treats a skill document as a structured retrieval target rather than one opaque text blob: it parses capabilities, parameters, and examples into a Skill Knowledge Graph, then generates capability-grounded pseudo-queries for offline index augmentation, online query expansion, or retriever training.
analysis.problem: Large skill libraries create an asymmetric retrieval problem: users describe goals colloquially while skill documents describe developer-facing capabilities, parameter schemas, and examples. Plain document-level pseudo-query generation can be topically related while missing the exact capability boundary or producing invalid parameters.
analysis.core_idea: Parse each skill into a graph over capabilities, parameters, and examples; imitate user-query style from examples, generate capability-specific query templates, fill and statically validate parameter slots, then use the resulting pseudo-queries as offline index augmentation, online expansion, or supervision for a dense/reranking SkillRouter.

memory_design.write: Skill documents already exist as persistent procedural artifacts; Skill2Query preprocesses them into a Skill Knowledge Graph and generates validated pseudo-queries attached to specific capabilities/parameters.
memory_design.organize: Represent each skill with structured Capability, Parameter, and Example nodes so synthetic queries can be tied to a concrete functional point instead of only the full-document semantics.
memory_design.read: At retrieval time, use generated pseudo-queries through offline index expansion, online query expansion, or a retriever trained on synthetic query-skill pairs; the selected skill is then injected into the downstream agent prompt.
memory_design.update_forget: The paper does not study lifelong skill updates or forgetting; pseudo-query generation and retriever training are primarily offline/index-time operations, with online expansion as an optional query-time mode.

compared_to: plain sparse/dense skill retrieval without generated queries
Zero-shot, Few-shot, and SkillFlow-style document-level pseudo-query generation
BM25, dense SR-Emb, and two-stage SkillRouter retrieval with baseline/offline/online variants
analysis.evidence: Across retrieval settings the paper reports an average Recall@1 gain of 6.70 points. On ToolQA, offline Skill2Query raises SkillRouter R@1 from 35.80% to 47.34% and SR-Emb R@1 from 13.22% to 29.79%; on TheoremQA, online BM25 expansion raises R@1 from 60.37% to 65.19%, but online expansion hurts several LogicBench/ToolQA settings, showing that offline and online augmentation are not uniformly beneficial. In the generation ablation, removing the Skill Knowledge Graph drops Exec-Pass from 42.85% to 22.63% and functional coverage from 11.32% to 2.41%. A 747-instance TheoremQA case study shows the fine-tuned SkillRouter improving task success over no skill by +3.48pp (GPT-5.4), +8.57pp (DeepSeek-V4-Flash), and +3.34pp (Qwen3.6-Plus).
analysis.why_it_matters: The paper sharpens the skill-retrieval interface: 'relevance' needs capability and parameter grounding, not just semantic similarity. It also exposes a deployment trade-off between precomputed semantic bridging and online adaptive expansion. For the radar, the important point is narrower than a new memory architecture: retrieval quality for procedural memory can be improved by exploiting the internal structure of the stored skill artifact itself.
limitations: The end-to-end execution study is a one-step TheoremQA case study rather than long-horizon tool execution across diverse environments.
Online query expansion is inconsistent and degrades some retrieval settings, so the paper does not establish one universally superior serving mode.
Performance depends on standardized skill documentation with explicit parameters/examples; poorly documented open skill ecosystems may erase the advantage.
The work targets retrieval over an existing skill library rather than memory writing, consolidation, evolution, or lifecycle governance.
